In other words, five months into the fiscal year, before all the figures are in, the budget for Environment Canada is already $20 million more than the budget for the entire year in which the Liberals were last in office.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the serious cuts in the National Research Council was that of the special research group into PBCs which was cut early in the mandate of the Government. Had that cut not been made this country would be in a far better position today to deal with this serious problem.

I will direct my question to the Prime Minister again. Why did the Prime Minister this year eliminate the program to construct federal sewage treatment facilities? Why, for four years, has the Government consistently refused the requests of every city and town in the country to provide federal help in a co-operative fashion to
Oral Questions
eliminate the dumping of raw sewage into our lakes, rivers, and streams?
Why has he refused to enter the cost-sharing program proposed by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities to meet anti-pollution standards, to deal with raw sewage, and to eliminate the problem of pollution in our great metropolitan areas? speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hypocrisy of the Official Opposition has no boundaries. The fact is that when the Liberal Party was in office in the late 1970s and early 1980s it cancelled broadly-based national programs to fund provinces and, through provinces, municipalities for waste water treatment. That program was done away with by the Liberals.
In the absence of that program, when we took office, we resorted to very innovative ways to clean up the St. Lawrence River, for which purpose the federal Cabinet approved $110 million. Recently we announced, with the Province of Nova Scotia, a $197.5 million program to clean up the Halifax Harbour. The list goes on.
In fact, if you add to the budget of the Department of the Environment all the expenditures on the environment of DRIE, Energy, Mines and Resources, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, and the Office of Western Diversification, not only have we kept up with inflation, we have also exceeded it in expenditures on the environment.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also addressed to the Minister of the Environment who last week, here in Ottawa, endorsed transportable incinerators for the destruction of PCBs.
Will the Minister confirm the statement by Tom Meredith, President of ENSCO, that such incinerators would only be set up at a single site in Ontario, in Quebec and in the Maritimes, so that PCBs would be brought to each incinerator site? Would the Minister confirm Mr. Meredith's statement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the gentleman to whom the Hon. Member makes reference was expressing a point of view, albeit a very expert one. The details surrounding any leasing of a portable or transportable unit for the incineration of PCBs remain to be finalized. I am consulting with my cabinet colleagues on the question, in concert with the provinces.
There are very formidable obstacles facing all the provinces in connection with the establishment of even a transportable unit, not to mention a permanent one. But I can assure the Hon. Member for Davenport, and through him, all Members of the House, that the Government of Canada is treating the

September 13, 1988
Oral Questions
issue with utmost urgency, and any technical or other obstacles to doing the job will, we hope, be overcome.

Mr. Speaker, in 1985, in an announcement made by the Department of the Environment, the following statement was made: "The federal Government announced in May 1985 that it will take the lead in arranging for mobile treatment facilities". What has happened to that commitment of the Minister's Government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the commitment was pretty well honoured. We had a fairly broadly based strategy when the Ministers of the Environment met in 1985 to deal with many facets of PCB management in the country. For example, it was that very strategy which gave rise to the building in Swan Hills, Alberta, of a permanent facility for PCB incineration, which plant we hope to have on stream in October if all the relevant environmental tests are passed and the permit is granted by the province.
In connection with the same strategy, we brought on stream many units across the country for the incineration of low-level PCB contaminated material. We have encountered quite a bit of resistance in Quebec and Ontario to the building of permanent facilities for the same purpose, but we are trying to overcome those obstacles by pursuing with the United States the possible leasing of transportable units.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CRIMINAL CODE APPLY TO ENVIRONMENT LEGISLATION VIOLATIONS
REQUEST THAT CRIMINAL CODE APPLY TO ENVIRONMENT LEGISLATION VIOLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister said just over a week ago that the nation needs what he described as a collective commitment to deal with the serious environmental problems. Given that the people of Canada are waiting for the Government of Canada to catch up to them in their concern about the environment, will this newly expressed concern lead to concrete action?
I think specifically of the following. A year before the Government brought in its Bill, allegedly to protect the environment, the Law Reform Commission made a report to the federal Government urging it to put crimes against the environment in the Criminal Code of Canada.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister why the Government of Canada rejected this advice when it drafted its legislation for June? And will it now change its position on this important issue, catch up to the people of Canada, and put environmental concerns in the Criminal Code?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CRIMINAL CODE APPLY TO ENVIRONMENT LEGISLATION VIOLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have already indicated, I think my hon. friend would agree that the actions of the Government in passing the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, in developing with the provinces some five new national parks, and in concluding
some important international treaties on behalf of the protection of the environment, have been useful and important contributions to the national well-being with respect to the protection of the environment.
No one has a monopoly on virtue. No one has a monopoly on his or her desire to protect a heritage or the environment. I think all Members of the House of Commons feel very strongly about the protection of the environment, and it is in our interest to act wisely and collectively to ensure that it be done.
We have taken some important measures. We propose to take more. I listened with care and attention to my hon. friend as he made some important suggestions with respect to the protection of the environment.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CRIMINAL CODE APPLY TO ENVIRONMENT LEGISLATION VIOLATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the point is that these suggestions have been made by this Party not just in recent weeks but over the past number of years. More concretely, from the Government's point of view, it was the Law Reform Commission of Canada, which reports to the federal Government, that made the same suggestion.

subtopic: INCLUSION OF CRIMES AGAINST ENVIRONMENT IN CRIMINAL CODE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
INCLUSION OF CRIMES AGAINST ENVIRONMENT IN CRIMINAL CODE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Other countries in the world, including Japan, West Germany, Switzerland and Denmark, and more than 10 states in the United States have already made the decision to include crimes against the environment in the Criminal Code. My question for the Prime Minister is simple. Why does the Canadian Government not agree with this very constructive action?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: INCLUSION OF CRIMES AGAINST ENVIRONMENT IN CRIMINAL CODE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party should know that the new Canadian Environmental Protection Act contains very severe sanctions. There are enshrined in the very fabric of the legislation sanctions that are akin to those he is calling for. Indeed, those sanctions include $1 million a day fines, and chief executive officers and presidents themselves are personally held liable in the eyes of the law for offences committed by their agents, their companies, or by themselves. There are six-month jail sentences and up to five-year jail sentences among the sanctions.
The Hon. Leader of the NDP asks why the sanctions were not included in the Criminal Code. We were advised that while that might have made good rhetoric and, in the case of the Hon. Leader of the NDP, good demagoguery, the fact is it would have been much more difficult for the Crown to establish onus of proof following the path he has suggested than the one we actually took.
In the Canadian Environmental Protection Act we have the first major overhaul in environmental law since 1971. Those sanctions, by any reasonable standards, are tough and will be stringently enforced.
September 13, 1988

Mr. Speaker, I know the Minister has promised to swoop down at the appropriate time, but he also knows that these tough standards to which he is alluding do not exist. They have to be agreed to by the provinces. They have not had them agreed to yet. He knows that the one way of effectively dealing with the matter to ensure that the people of Saint-Basile-le-Grand and people in Vancouver, Charlottetown, or in Moose Jaw are equally protected by high standards, is to follow the Law Reform Commission's recommendation to put those standards in the Criminal Code.
Will the Minister deal with the substance of that matter now? Will he acknowledge he could have put this matter in the Criminal Code, like other countries in the world have done? He could have had those high standards. Why didn't he do it? And why won't he do it in the future?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is not even unanimity within the Law Reform Commission. It is very debatable within the legal community that the best way to go is through the Criminal Code. The best experts whose advice we could draw on indicated to us that we would be able to get convictions and we would be able to throw the polluters in jail more effectively and expeditiously if we followed a different course.
We have very tough sanctions. There are $1 million a day fines. In some categories there are no limits available to the judiciary for this purpose. There are stiff jail sentences as an option, six-month jail sentences for some offences and five-year sentences in other cases. We think we can get the convictions more effectively on the path we have taken than on the one the Hon. Leader of the NDP has suggested for purely partisan and political reasons.

ASSISTANCE FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM-SIZED BUSINESSES- GOVERNMENT POSITION

maintopic: TRUCKING INDUSTRY DEREGULATION-REQUEST FOR FREEZE ON SERVICES
TRUCKING INDUSTRY DEREGULATION-REQUEST FOR FREEZE ON SERVICES
speechtext:

During discussions on the White Paper, Freedom to Move, and the subsequent legislation implementing deregulation of transportation, the Conservative Government was warned time and time again that it would be creating chaos out of stability, particularly in trucking. With the demise of Transport Route, which was formerly CN Route, and the loss of up to 2,400 jobs, we are seeing the inevitable results of deregulation.
Will the Government act immediately to freeze existing trucking routes and services and, as soon as possible, restore stability to the trucking industry by reintroducing the test of public convenience and necessity?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry St. Germain (Minister of State (Transport)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is being totally unfair when he brings regulatory reform into the picture. -and those who are involved. I have asked my colleagues, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Minister of Labour, and the Minister of State for Finance to assess the situation immediately in terms
of Transport Route Canada. This Government will make sure that the interests of workers are looked after.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry St. Germain (Minister of State (Transport)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, here again I think we have to put this in the proper context.
A rip-off.

Government to clean up the environment by reducing the volume of garbage that is produced by requiring federally regulated companies to recycle their garbage, and at the same time impose packaging restrictions which would require packaging to be bio-degradable?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:

maintopic: RAFFERTY-ALAMEDA DAM-STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO FORMER OFFICIAL
RAFFERTY-ALAMEDA DAM-STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO FORMER OFFICIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Miss Elizabeth May, a distinguished environmental expert in this country, recently a senior adviser on the environment in the Minister's office, has resigned her position on the grounds that the Minister of the Environment made a political deal to grant a licence for the Rafferty-Alameda dam project in Saskatchewan, which will have an enormous impact on the province of Manitoba, without undertaking any studies or any environmental impact assessments whatsoever, in return for which the federal Government would receive provincial agreement for a grasslands national park, and to use the statement of Miss May: "Manitoba's interests have . . . been shafted".
If this is true, it represents a serious violation of public trust in the Minister's responsibilities. Is the Prime Minister prepared to undertake an inquiry immediately into the charges made by Miss May, based upon the major credibility that she has as an environmental expert in this country, to determine why the Minister was prepared to make a deal that would grant federal approval for a licence for a project in the riding of the Premier of Saskatchewan in return for a provincial agreement on a park, and put at mercy the environment of Manitoba for the sake of a political deal? Does the Prime Minister not agree that that warrants a proper inquiry by the Government into the actions and behaviour of this Minister?

September 13, 1988
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
maintopic: RAFFERTY-ALAMEDA DAM-STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO FORMER OFFICIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no foundation whatever to the charge that the Hon. Member has just made. The premise of the question is that "Manitoba's interests were shafted" in connection with the permit issued by me under the authority of the International River Improvements Act.
I have an article in my hand from the Winnipeg Free Press that quotes the former Deputy Environment Minister, Tom Owen, who, I gather, was in office at the time. He stated: "Manitoba officials were not concerned because they viewed an agreement between Canada and the United States that governs the transborder flow of water as the province's best safeguard. That opposition to the licence was not a position we the Manitoba Government took".

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Minister can slough this one off. The fact of the matter is that a senior adviser in his own office, who gave him advice on environmental matters, has resigned her position on the grounds that the Minister deliberately betrayed the trust of his office by granting a licence without doing an environmental impact study on a project that will see interbasin transfers of waters, a position that all parties took when it affected the Garrison diversion, and this Minister has granted a licence without that type of study. Even the Government of the Province of Manitoba today states that it has written to the Minister asking that the project be delayed in return for proper studies.
Will the Minister undertake to halt any further agreement on this project, and state that agreement will not be granted until there is a proper impact study on the waters of Manitoba and what the project will do to them, or is the Minister already too deeply embedded in his political deal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I made my decision to grant the permit for the Rafferty dam, I had in my office my Deputy Minister, my senior Assistant Deputy Minister for this area, and the top hydrologist in the Government of Canada in my own Department, and I asked them, after many meetings over many weeks, what was their best advice. They said: "Minister, our best advice is that you have no technical or other grounds on which to refuse the permit. We recommend that 13 environmental conditions, all of them stringent, be attached to the permit. Our advice to you is that if any one of them is not honoured by the relevant jurisdictions (a) you have the power to revoke the permit, and (b) you ought to do so".
I acquiesced in the advice of my top officials. I think it was the right decision, and I would do it again.

Mr. Speaker, surely the Minister knows that his issuing of this permit without adequate environmental study belies a lot of the
rhetoric that the Prime Minister and the Minister have been spouting this last week about a new commitment to the environment.
This was a serious breach of the Minister's responsibility to issue that permit. In the letter he quoted from Manitoba the Minister referred to the Canada-U.S. Boundaries Waters Treaty. It is precisely in the context of that treaty that he has been asked before in the House to refer the matter to the International Joint Commission for a study, which he has not been prepared to do.
I ask the Minister if he will commission the appropriate studies, and stop kidding us by saying that there are these 13 environmental conditions that have to be met. We all know that once a dam is built and water is polluted in Manitoba there is now way of revoking that. We want studies done now, not after the fact.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand, and I will share it with the Hon. Member or anybody else in the House, a history of the Rafferty dam going back to the 1930s. It has been studied to death ever since. Different Governments of different political Parties have sought the construction of this project.
I made my decision based on the advice of the best hydrologists in the country and of most senior officials. I note that these questions are based on an article that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press which contains a paragraph that the Opposition does not quote. It states: "Miss May said she hopes environmental groups don't take a knee-jerk anti-Tory stance because I do think they, the federal Tories, deserve credit for having done more in the federal environment area than any previous federal Government".

Mr. Speaker, it would not take much to supersede the record of the former Liberal Government, by anyone's admission. That is not what is at stake here.
What is at stake here is the Manitoba environment and the fact that the Minister has seriously compromised his credibility with respect to a serious environmental question by issuing that permit against the advice of his senior environmental expert.
The Minister talked about not having any good technical reasons to turn down the permit. There are a lot of good environmental reasons to turn down the project. That is what the Minister has failed to consider, and that is why he should no longer be the Minister of the Environment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have obligations under the International Rivers Improvements Act to ensure that any project that affects a river that is jointly managed by different jurisdictions,
September 13, 1988

including not only Canada but the United States, meets the most rigorous environmental standards.
I have satisfied myself on the basis of advice from the best experts that I could consult that those obligations are being met. The Province of Saskatchewan approved the dam. The Province of Manitoba approved the dam. The State of North Dakota approved the dam. The Government of the United States approved the dam, and now the Government of Canada has approved the dam.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT- CANADIAN FEDERATION OF AGRICULTURE
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT- CANADIAN FEDERATION OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:

speechtext:

not been put on the import control list? Why has there been no arrangement established by the Minister for consultation as demanded by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture? Why has there been no action in this regard for the largest agricultural umbrella group in the country?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Last week witnesses from approximately 40 groups appeared before a committee. speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):

Mr. Speaker, I thank Hon. Members for their consent.
On March 25, 1986, I announced that effective December 31, 1992, the petroleum industry would be required to eliminate lead in gasoline across Canada.
My decision was based on a study conducted for Environment Canada by a blue ribbon panel of scientists under the direction of the Royal Society of Canada. Those experts recommended, among other things, that the Minister of the Environment consider even more stringent controls on leaded gasoline, should future research render such a course advisable.
Since that time new research in the United States and in Australia, and elsewhere has convinced me and the Government of Canada as a whole that lead in the environment poses an even more serious threat to human health, especially among children, than health experts previously thought.
Accordingly, I am announcing today, on behalf of the federal Cabinet, that lead in gasoline will be illegal at all retail outlets across Canada after December 1, 1990. Violators will be subject to very stiff sanctions under the new Canadian Environmental Protection Act.

Mr. Speaker, the statement by the Minister which we welcome fails to recognize that it was a Liberal Government that launched in December, 1983 the program of reducing and eventually eliminating lead in gasoline. This Government has now changed its position. Originally, probably yielding to pressures by industry, it decided to choose 1993 as the target year.
We in the Opposition have raised this matter in this House on a number of occasions. As recently as one month ago we called on the Government, on the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), and on the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to advance to 1990 the deadline for further reduction of lead in gasoline. We are glad, therefore, to see once more that the Government is continuing the work started by preceding Liberal Governments. What strikes us, though, as a bit disturbing is the timing of this announcement. It is

almost cynical or, I should say, almost a desperate attempt by this Conservative Government to gain credibility, to appear to be concerned with environment and with health. It is an attempt, in a way, of a blue chameleon trying to change its colour into green.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the announcement that the removal of lead from gasoline will be speeded up. It is something for which I have called for some time. Previous environment critics for the New Democratic Party caucus have called for it and, of course, environmentalists have called for it for a very long time.
I think that there is an easy, broader lesson to be learned. Reference has been made to the fact that experts have only recently found out that low levels of lead can be very harmful, particularly to the development of children. Yet, we have other environmental hazards which we are still seeing accumulate, on the basis that low levels are not harmful to health. I think that emissions of NOx, for example, are continuing to go up even with improved standards. There is still going to be an increase.
The Government has announced that low level radiation is not a health hazard. We wonder how many lives have to be lost and how much illness there has to be before the lesson is truly going to be learned that we have very serious environmental problems.
I welcome the announcement. It is high time that we move on leaded gasoline. It is particularly a problem in my area, an urban riding which has lead in the soil that is being removed. It is very, very significant in all areas of life, and it is still not being acted upon.

speechtext:
that Bill C-152, an Act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise today to speak to Bill C-152 and to open the debate on behalf of the Government. I am sure that it would be appropriate, Mr. Speaker, to let you and Members of the House know why I am standing in
this place this afternoon instead of the Hon. Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Weiner). I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you and Members would appreciate that this is one of the holy days of the faith that the Hon. Minister observes. For that reason he has asked me to make a presentation on behalf of the Government, and I am honoured to do so. I know that Hon. Members opposite will understand why he is not here.
Some two months ago, this House gave its unanimous consent to the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, and on July 21, Royal Assent passed this historic Act into law. I think all Members, and especially Government Members, are justifiably proud of the co-operation and consensus which turned this piece of Canadian legislation into the first law of its kind in the world.
This afternoon, in introducing for second reading Bill C-152, an Act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute, I believe it is a further demonstration of the viability and of the life that comes not only from the Multiculturalism Act but which is Canada.
Others Members of the House and I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that you have worked strenuously over the years in the field of multiculturalism, both as a Member of Parliament, as an active member of an ethnic group in Canada, and as a former Minister. I hope that you, as well as other Members of the House, feel that this is an important milestone in some of the work that you have done as well.
The Bill before us has its roots in the Canadian Multiculturalism Act and in the multiculturalism policy of Canada. This Bill gives expression to Section 3, subsection 1 of the Act, which states that it is the policy of the Government of Canada to preserve and enhance the use of languages other than English and French. This Bill also gives specific recognition to sections of the Canadian Multiculturalism Act which commit the Government to facilitate the acquisition, retention, and use of all languages that contribute to Canada's multicultural identity.
This Bill is another concrete example of our Government's resolve to meet the challenges of our evolving multicultural society which we set out in the Canadian Multiculturalism Act. Last year, the former Secretary of State, the Hon. David Crombie, announced the Government's intention to establish a national heritage languages institute in Edmonton. He commissioned Dr. Henry Kreisel of the University of Alberta and Dr. Michael Batts of the University of British Columbia to conduct a study on the best way to meet this commitment. The Bill before us today results from that cross-country process of consultation and assessment.
Dr. Kreisel recommended that the federal Government establish an institute to foster and further the learning of heritage languages, an institute that was described as without walls, an institute that would serve the needs of all those active in this area. The report recommended that the institute reach
September 13, 1988

out to the educational and cultural communities of Canada, to the business communities of Canada, and to all levels of government to forge a strong national network, a network bringing together linguistic resources of Canada and the experts in the field. It would in fact fulfil a tremendous need for the co-ordination and exchange of information on Canada's heritage languages.
I would like to take just a moment to emphasize to the Elouse the extent to which our heritage languages enrich the Canadian way of life. There are over 70 languages spoken in this country, not including specific dialects. Some belong to the aboriginal peoples of Canada and were part of our heritage long before the arrival of Europeans. Other languages have been brought to this nation by those who came here from all parts of the world seeking a land of freedom, security and opportunity.
From my own perspective, heritage languages are a vital component of daily life in Canada. I have spent considerable time travelling across the country and meeting people from many different cultural and racial groups, groups which remain fiercely proud of their first languages. One does not have to venture far in any of our major metropolitan centres to encounter the variety and the vitality of Canada's spoken languages. They are all around us. They are a living culture which lifts the everyday life of this country beyond the ordinary.
Just last Saturday, I had the opportunity to speak at the annual meeting of the Canadian German Congress in Winnipeg about the establishment of a chair for German-Canadian studies at the University of Winnipeg. This further verifies the multicultural nature of Canada and the need to preserve and give understanding to other Canadians of that heritage.
This richness and diversity of languages is something to be proud of. It is something to be cherished. It gives us a sense of where we have come from, a sense of our roots, and of how many unique individual heritages contribute to our national character.
Language is the strong current of a culture. Language provides the means for passing on the heart and soul of a culture, its folklore, stories of the past, and, yes, dreams of the future. Languages bond people together, giving them a strong sense of community and of common values, but languages are more than just a social phenomenon. Languages are an important natural resource for Canadian people.
Language is an economic resource. It is a resource which boosts our trading profile. It is a resource to use in international diplomacy. It is a resource for tourism. Certainly our reputation for hospitality and friendliness is much enhanced as we welcome visitors in the languages of the world. Within Canada today, there is an increasing demand for people- teachers, translators, negotiators-with heritage language skills. This is why we made such strong commitments in the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, commitments that we are backing up today with Bill C-152.
Canadian Heritage Languages Institute Act
Let me take a moment to outline to the House the special features of this legislation. The Bill describes the establishment of a new and special kind of institute, an institute which from the outset is designed to be a co-operative venture. We want the institute to be a facilitator, to be a means for community groups, institutions, corporations, and all levels of government to work together to develop the rich linguistic versatility of our society. To that end, we have established measures for an endowment fund, a fund which will allow the institute to function independently and to set its own priorities.
The institute will be incorporated federally as a charitable organization so that it can seek a broad base of public and private support. We also expect it to encourage support from other levels of government. I think all Hon. Members would see this as being a co-operative era of partnership in multiculturalism. This is our idea of working in co-operation with all segments of Canadian society and further developing a major national resource, our heritage languages.
The institute's mandate is ambitious. It will undertake a variety of activities that will foster the teaching and learning of heritage languages across Canada and their ongoing use in our society. This mandate includes improving public understanding and appreciation of heritage languages, upgrading the quality of instruction and learning materials, developing Canadian oriented materials, and conducting research into all aspects of Canada's heritage languages. Of course, one major purpose of the institute is to provide a national focus, a focus which will bring together expertise from across the country to respond to the different priorities identified at the community level.
I will not take the time of the House now to go into specifics about the powers of the institute or the way it will be set up. There might be questions about that later. Each of us here has an opportunity to read and to consider the Bill, but I wish to make the point that it is important for all of us to consider, in a positive sense, our heritage languages.
We have attempted to provide the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute with the maximum degree of flexibility, the flexibility to ensure that it can meet its objectives and achieve excellence in its work. We have given the institute a structure and a set of objectives to accomplish this important task. Let me repeat just how important this task is.
Right now, the multiculturalism sector of the Department of the Secretary of State supports some 1,600 supplementary schools at which over 130,000 students have a chance to learn the languages of their ancestors. These are impressive figures and enrolments are continuing to rise. My point is that we are not dealing with a marginal social and cultural activity. We are in fact responding to the many Canadians who feel deeply concerned about preserving their heritage languages and using them in today's modern society. We have made a commitment to help these Canadians do exactly that.
Our commitment to this institute is part of the strong new directions for multiculturalism that were announced last May by the Minister. That commitment is being reinforced with

September 13, 1988
Message from the Senate
$62 million in new money over the next five years, including $14.5 million to preserve and enhance heritage languages and culture. Over the first five years of its existence the institute will receive $6.7 million. What is significant is the breakdown of this funding to ensure a sound base for the institute's development and long-term financial security.
In addition to $250,000 start up financing, $500,000 per year will be provided for operating costs and $800,000 per year will go to a special endowment fund. This fund is designed to help the institute become financially self-sufficient in keeping with our fiscal responsibilities to the Canadian taxpayers.
I should also take some time to address the question of the relationship between heritage languages and official languages. The Canadian Multiculturalism Act clearly states that it is the policy of the Government of Canada to preserve and enhance the use of languages other than English and French while strengthening the status and use of the official languages of Canada. I am proud to say that our Government's record speaks for itself in this regard. It is our Government that brought in the new Official Languages Act. It is my colleague from Lac-Saint-Jean, the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard), who negotiated landmark agreements on official languages with a number of provinces. The Bill we are considering today complements those agreements. Most important, it complements our official languages policy by advancing multiculturalism throughout Canada in harmony with a national commitment to our official languages.
I think it should be noted that the Secretary of State, who has responsibility under the Financial Administration Act for official languages and for these programs, is of French Canadian background. The Minister who brought forward the Multiculturalism Act and the Heritage Languages Act has an ethnic background, if I can use that term. That is simply a demonstration of the fact that all of us here have different experiences and backgrounds. Whether our experiences are personal in the sense that our families came from other countries, or whether it is simply through our knowledge of history, those experiences are very much part of our lives today.
That fact also reminds me of the story my father told me, something which might be reflected in various ways by other Canadians. He came to this country in 1924 as a medical doctor, never to practise again, because of the history of Europe involving World War I and the Russian civil war and revolution. He arrived in Quebec City, speaking five languages and none of them was official. However, he was accepted into Canada. He was given freedom and the right to practise religion as we saw fit. We were given the right to speak our own languages. Above all, we were given the opportunity to develop not only our families and communities but hopefully also contribute to the development of Canada.
I have used that personal vignette simply to make the point that there are Canadians across our land who have had if not the same experience at least similar experiences and it indicates why Canada is so important to them.
Heritage languages are a vital element of communication and understanding in our multicultural society. They are fundamental to the way in which we deal with one another as Canadians. I truly believe that this country has an unlimited opportunity with its people, its cultural diversity, and many different languages, to take greater advantage of this modern world than any other country. To do so we must safeguard and develop what we have. We must look to the future with a sure sense of where we are going. This Bill is part of that progressive outlook. I hope the House will give it rapid passage in order that the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute can begin its work without further delay.
If I may be permitted, let me say in the other language that I speak: Vielen danke fur die gelegenheit, heute zu sprechen zu diese wichtige sache. I hope we get passage soon.

The second reason for supporting the principle of the institute is, as the Minister well noted, that the question of heritage languages is very much alive and well in Canadian society. There are some 128,000 children enrolled in various language programs across the country spanning some 62 languages. The census figures of 1986 indicate that many Canadians of various generations are not speaking only English and French but are trying to maintain a third or fourth language, not only as an inherent part of their culture but also in an attempt to broaden their opportunities by possessing one or more languages.
My own riding of York West reflects that dynamism. The last census indicated that 37,000 individuals in York West alone spoke a mother tongue other than other English or French. These tongues include Italian, German, Chinese, Ukrainian, and Portuguese, as well as a number of other languages. In York West individuals are trying to keep these languages alive as a part of identifying their cultural roots and identity which give us all a sense of purpose and vision. There is a link between language preservation and cultural preservation. One without the other is certainly poorer for it.
The third reason we believe it is important to rally behind the principle of an institute is that we believe we should view heritage languages in a constructive sense and as a national resource and treasure. We should adopt a philosophy that in addition to our bilingualism policy of English and French, it is an advantage to be able to speak a third or fourth language. It is an advantage to utilize a third or fourth language to delve deeper into one's culture or to open locked doors which will remain locked without the knowledge of another language. As a country we should be adopting that as a positive tool.
In my travels as a Member of Parliament on various parliamentary committees I have always been pleasantly surprised by the different school systems in the different parts of the world where children are encouraged to learn three languages. More than a cultural attribute, they realize that a youngster graduating from school will possess an economic
