PROCEEDINGS REGARDING LEONARD PELTIER Mr. Jim Fulton (Skeena) moved:
That this House deplores the extradition of Mr. Leonard Peltier to the United States from Canada on the basis of false information filed with a Canadian court by American authorities, and that this House calls upon the government to seek the return of Mr. Peltier to Canada and the annulment of all extradition proceedings in this regard.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to again have an opportunity to bring the Leonard Peltier matter before the House. I think there are very clear parallels between this case and the case of a perhaps more well known Canadian, Donald Marshall, and the inquiry into what really went on when an innocent native Canadian was held for so many years when he was absolutely innocent of the charge of which he was convicted.
September 13, 1988

Leonard Peltier is presently being held in Leavenworth Penitentiary, Kansas, and for those members of the public who are interested in looking at more of the precise legal arguments with respect to this case, they can find them beginning at page 5025 of Hansard of April 9, 1987, when a large number of Members of this House participated in the debate on what was then known as Motion M-28.
The treaty was broken by the United States in the Peltier matter. That treaty is a very old one, established between Canada and the U.S. on August 9, 1842. It was amended July 12, 1889. It is Article 9 that I am specifically addressing in relation to the motion presently before the House today. If one looks at Article 9 of the treaty, one sees that there is a requirement that the prima facie evidence put before the courts of another country be provided in an honest, factual, forthright manner by the foreign country party to the treaty. Otherwise serious damage is done to the treaty, obviously. In this case, serious damage is done to the highest courts of Canada, the Supreme Court of British Columbia, the Government and people of Canada, and most obviously to Leonard Peltier who is presently serving two concurrent life sentences for an offence which it is unlikely that he committed.
There is a basic legal argument that all the evidence, not just the Myrtle Poor Bear affidavits, had no validity. There was no evidence sufficient to warrant Peltier's extradition in 1976 to stand trial on charges of murder. Evidence advanced in support of extradition, apart from the fabricated affidavits, does no more than place Peltier with several others hours after the probable time of the shoot out. This counters the current Minister of Justice's position that "the evidence held against Mr. Peltier was considered sufficient to warrant committal for extradition on four of the five charges contained in the extradition request".
The extradition was successfully obtained by fraud committed by agents of the Government of the United States against the Government of Canada and the Supreme Court of British Columbia. The basic argument is that evidence obtained by fraud is no evidence. The legal argument and challenge to us as Members of this House and Canadians generally is that the "impugned extradition" should be declared null and void so the U.S. Government is not permitted to retain the benefit of its own fraud, which in this case is the damage done to Canada and the continued incarceration of Mr. Peltier.
There are certain basic facts which should be on the record, and then I intend to quote from a number of articles written by a large number of journalists on this matter in recent months. The facts are that on June 18, 1976, Mr. Justice Schultz of the Supreme Court of British Columbia granted an order to the Government of the United States of America for the extradition of Leonard Peltier on, inter alia, two counts of first degree murder.
Extradition
Second, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal without written reasons on October 27, 1976. The applicant was extradited on December 18 after an unsuccessful appeal to the Minister of Justice.
Third, the order put the applicant on trial for the murder of special agents Ronald Williams and Jack Coler of the Federal Bureau of Investigation at the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota, U.S.A., on June 26, 1975. The applicant was convicted on both counts at Fargo, North Dakota, on April 18, 1977.
In October, 1987, the Supreme Court of the United States refused to hear an application for a new trial, exhausting all available domestic legal remedies. The applicant was also extradited by the State of Wisconsin on a charge of attempted murder and by the State of Oregon on a charge of burglary. He was acquitted on the charge of attempted murder and the charge of burglary was dismissed at the request of the prosecution.
The applicant was not ordered to be extradited on a count of attempted murder of an Oregon state policeman on November 14, 1975, on the ground that the details of the incident was scanty and the identification of the assailant weak, notwithstanding the deposition of Officer Kenneth T. Griffiths.
The extradition of Mr. Peltier was the result of a fraud perpetrated on the Government of Canada and the Supreme Court of British Columbia by agents of the Government of the United States in that it was based on affidavit evidence known by said agents to be false, and thus is void ab initio.
On October 1 of last year members of all three Parties joined together and held a press conference and released documents, those Members being the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), who is here and will, I imagine, participate in today's debate, myself, and the Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Suluk). The three of us have obviously reviewed many thousands of pages of documents in relation to Mr. Peltier and truly believe that the way in which to remedy the matter is through Motion 115 which is before us today.
On April 9, 1987, The Gazette ran an article entitled "Indian leader extradited via false evidence: lawyer". Lou Gurwitz, who was here for the debate last year, has for many years been Mr. Peltier's counsel. He described the conviction as "the clearest case of frame-up I've ever seen." That is a lawyer who has practised criminal law in the United States for many, many years.
Last year representative Don Edwards of the U.S. Congress and Chair of the House Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights stated that the evidence clearly indicated "government abuse of the investigative process, suppression of evidence and falsehood".

September 13, 1988
Extradition
The U.S. Government itself admitted that the affidavits used to extradite Leonard Peltier were entirely false. This prompted an article in the Yale Law Review, Volume II, number one in the fall of 1983 by J. J. Privitera in reference to Canada and the Peltier case. He said:
Implicit in any workable contract between nations in which they agree to submit evidence in support of probable cause to the courts of either state must be an understanding that the parties will not defraud one another.
There are many other articles, including several more recent ones from which I would like to quote. One was written by Kirk Makin for The Globe and Mail. He actually travelled to Kansas City where he interviewed Mr. Peltier at Leavenworth. The article reads:
Leonard Peltier is in the hole again, undergoing the worst punishment a prison can mete out.
But to the native Indian activist, it is almost like going home. For nine of his First 12 years in jail, Mr. Peltier languished in isolation in even worse conditions-23 hours a day in a two by 2.5-meter cell.
Yet Mr. Peltier's stature as a symbol of Indian oppression continues to grow. The next scene is due to unfold on a Canadian stage later this year. A team of lawyers is currently preparing several legal challenges.
In the main one, they will try to convince the Supreme Court of Canada that Mr. Peltier must be returned because the Federal Bureau of Investigation falsified evidence used to extradite him in 1976.
"It was not only Leonard Peltier's rights that were violated," Mr. Peltier said in a prison interview observed by two sour guards and a revolving camera. "It was the rights of all Canadian citizens.
"There was a fraud committed on the whole judicial system. The United States seems to have no respect for its allies."
Mr. Peltier's fame extends to Europe and Asia, and he has defence committees dotted all over. Thousands of Californians recently attended a benefit concert for his defence, and the Human Rights Commission of Spain recently awarded him the International Human Rights Prize.
Mr. Makins' article of June 3, 1988, continues:
The Canadian lawyers are also looking into a civil suit against the FBI, and into the possibility that Mr. Peltier has Canadian relatives might afford him Canadian Indian status, permitting him to be transferred to a Canadian prison.
"There is no question the legal focus has turned to Canada," Toronto lawyer Dianne Martin said. "And this is not some kind of show trial. It is the most time-consuming, exhausting project I have ever undertaken.
"We became party to a terrible injustice," she said. "Canada has an obligation to that man. We allowed ourselves to be used in the FBI's paranoid attack on American Indians.
June Callwood wrote an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail on October 21, 1987. She says:
In the fall 1976, Marlon Brando went to Ottawa to see Warren Allmand, who was then Minister of Indian affairs, to beg him to help obtain a new extradition hearing for an Ojibway-Dakota Indian, Leonard Peltier. The U.S. Government wanted the American Indian Movement leader to try him for the shoot-out deaths on June 26, 1975, of two FBI agents at the Harry Jumping Bull hall on the Pine Ridge reserve in South Dakota.
Leonard Peltier, a charismatic man who was leading a protest against the giveaway of Oglala Sioux reserve lands on which uranium had been discovered, was viewed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation as a dangerous person.
The agency was so anxious to bring him to trial that it falsified the evidence it presented at the extradition hearing in Vancouver, a fact that emerged in examination of the 12,000 relevant documents since obtained under the U.S.
Freedom of Information Act. The FBI's deceit at the hearing is no longer in dispute.
The critical evidence was given in a affidavit by Myrtle Poor Bear, an addled woman who had been hospitalized more than 100 times for mental illness. The FBI obtained from her five separate accounts of the shootings and chose the most damaging of these, the one in which she declared she watched Leonard Peltier kill the men at pointblank range. On the basis of that affidavit, a federal court of Canada sent Leonard Peltier back to the United States. The truth is that Myrtle Poor Bear was not present at the shootings.
Warren Allmand did not act on Marlon Brando's personal plea that the evidence at the extradition hearings had been concocted, and now he's a sorry man. Last April, the Montreal Liberal spoke in the House of Commons in support of a private member's bill, Motion 28, brought by James Fulton, the New Democrat member for Skeena. It asked that the Canadian Government request Washington to return the Indian leader to Canada, on the grounds that the extradition was obtained by fraudulence. Warren Allmand now describes the extradition as "a travesty of justice."
Motion 28 was, of course, talked out. A government engaged in a dimpled dance of courtship with the United States is not likely to prejudice its hope of coitus by rushing to assist a native person going blind in a Kansan prison.
Leonard Peltier, 42, is serving two life sentences in Leavenworth. An arterial hemorrhage threatens his sight. All appeal recourses have been exhausted, the last one only two weeks ago, despite proof that the evidence at his trial was poisoned and much that was favourable to him was suppressed.
It has been more than 13 years since two FBI agents turned up at the hall occupied by Leonard Peltier, two other men, and some women and children. Although the agents had no warrant, they said they wanted to search the premises for used cowboy boots they believed Jimmy Eagle, a 12-year-old boy, had stolen. Leonard Peltier, mindful that more than 400 native people had been killed on the reserve in recent years, resisted. Within minutes the place was swarming with state troopers. The National Guard, SWAT teams, the 82nd Airborne Division in helicopters, armed personal carriers and Ml6s.
The two FBI men and a native person died as thousands of rounds of ammunition shredded the building.
Four AIM members, including Leonard Peltier, were charged. Two went to trial for murder but were acquitted unanimously by juries critical of the FBI's evidence. The man the FBI really wanted, however, was Leonard Peltier, who had fled to Canada. He was arrested in Hinton, Alta., in February of 1976, and extradited in December, despite strong suspicion that he had been railroaded.
The support for Leonard Peltier is unprecedented and resembles that given Nelson Mandela of South Africa, with whom his name is often linked.
The White House has received petitions bearing more than 20 million signatures, 18 million of them from the Soviet Union, which views the native leader as a martyr to U.S. racism. Congressman Donald Edwards, a Californian democrat and a former FBI agent himself, joined 55 other Republican and Democratic Congressmen this year to seek a new trial for Leonard Peltier. In Canada, 60 Members of Parliament support the cause and so do 74 international church groups, Amnesty International, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Desmond Tutu of South Africa, George Erasmus of the National Indian Brotherhood and four Nobel Prize winners.
I think that gives some idea of the research that journalists have undertaken with respect to Leonard Peltier's case. The Sunday Star on May 10, 1987, published a short editorial which is worthy of being placed on the record. It is entitled "A subversion of due process".
A little known case involving an American Indian extradited from Canada to face murder charges in the United States is testing Canada's willingness to protect its judicial process from abuse by foreign countries.
The case involves Leonard Peltier, an American Indian leader alleged to have killed two FBI agents in 1975. Peltier was extradited after a 1976 Vancouver hearing. It has since been learned that U.S. authorities submitted
September 13, 1988

false evidence at the extradition hearing, but the Canadian Government has not demonstrated the will to protest.
However, Jim Fulton, a New Democratic Party MP from British Columbia has put forward a Private Member's Bill calling upon the Government to demand Peltier's return to Canada for a new hearing. Fulton points out that the key evidence at the 1976 hearing was an affidavit sworn by Myrtle Poor Bear, who said that she had observed Peltier shoot the FBI agents at point-blank range as they lay wounded behind a car. It has since been confirmed that the judge was not shown an earlier affidavit in which Poor Bear, a psychotic with a record of 105 hospital stays-admitted that she wasn't present when the agents were killed.
The Peltier case demonstrates how the authorities were able to take advantage of an extradition treaty in which the evidence consists of affidavits that must be accepted on blind faith and the accused person is not present at the hearing to offer a rebuttal.
Furthermore, under the terms of the treaty, the U.S. Government was represented at the Peltier hearing by a Canadian lawyer on the staff of the federal Department of Justice. This demonstrates the conflict of interest surrounding then Justice Minister Ron Basford's decision not to exercise his discretion to override the decision of the judge.
The Fulton Bill parallels an American effort to vindicate Peltier, now in his 11th year of imprisonment in the U.S. The Bill has the support of 60 MPs representing all three Parties. But it recently failed to come to a vote because of the limited time allotted for the debate of Private Members' Bills.
But the Government does not need the approval of Parliament before launching a protest over the use of false evidence to win Peltier's extradition. What is it waiting for?
I have another article with the headline "Evidence on Peltier was false, MP says", and other articles entitled "U.S. told lies in extradition case-lawyer", "MPs seek new hearing", "Indian leader extradited via false evidence: lawyer", "MP's Bill seeks return of Indian from U.S. jail". The articles go on and on. In October of 1986, The Ottawa Citizen published an article by Stephen Bindman entitled "Jailed Indian activist has new hope international clamour will set him free". The article is worthy of quoting as well:
Amnesty International, the human rights monitoring agency, has said "the interest of justice would best be served'' by giving Peltier a new trial because of "serious doubts'' about his first encounter with justice.
The National Association of Criminal Defence Lawyers in the U.S. has gone to bat for the native leader and the Chairman of the House of Representatives sub-committee on civil rights has said the Peltier case clearly indicated "government abuse of the investigative process, suppression of evidence and falsehood".
In his latest unsuccessful appeal, three judges of 8th U.S. circuit court of appeal conceded last month that the prosecution had withheld ballistic evidence at the trial which was favourable to Peltier.
"There is a possibility that the jury would have acquitted Leonard Peltier had the records and data improperly withheld from the defence been available to him," the judges said.
They also said there was clear evidence in the case of "improper conduct on the part of some FBI agents".
But the judges said that under guidelines issued by the Supreme Court, a possibility is not enough to order a new trial, there must be a probability.
I think Members of this House need to understand what those guidelines of the U.S. Supreme Court mean to someone like Leonard Peltier.
Said Peltier's New York Lawyer William Kundstler: "Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse had the seventh Calgary and Leonard Peltier now has the 8th circuit.
Extradition
"There can be no rational explanation of this ruling other than that the court was unwilling to grant a new trial, no matter how justified, in a case involving the death of two FBI agents".
I have another article written by Michele Landsberg from New York. It was published in The Globe and Mail on June 14, 1986. Again, it is worthy of being placed on the record.
Looking back 10 years Vancouver Lawyer Don Rosenbloom called the extradition of Leonard Peltier "the most disgusting experience of my life".
Saul Terry, president of the B.C. Union of Indian Chiefs, remembers the
case as "sleazy".
Right Rev. Robert Smith, moderator of the United Church of Canada, calls it "a shadow (across) the national conscience of Canada".
And I call it terrifying.
The more I plow through the documents in the case of Mr. Peltier, the more chillingly I am reminded that legislators and law enforcers are capable of every kind of treachery, and that Canada, the bland and the good, has been party to a fraud.
If that seems extreme, let me backtrack to June, 1975, to Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. The U.S. Government was virtually at war- complete with armed men and heavy weaponry-against American Indian movement dissidents camped on the reserve. AIM was there to protest against the tribal chief, who was busily selling one-eighth of the reserve lands, rich in oil and uranium, to the federal Government.
The FBI committed a fraud as the U.S. Government later admitted (but only after it had Mr. Peltier back in its grasp) and on the basis of that fraud, the Canadian judge ordered Mr. Peltier's extradition. Mr. Rosenbloom desperately flew to Ottawa to ask the then Minister of Justice, Ron Basford, to stay the extradition on the grounds that the affidavit was now known to be false. Mr. Basford refused.
It is at this point that one must wonder about the propriety of having one of Mr. Basford's staff representing the U.S. Government. Is there not even a ghost of a suspicion that there could be a conflict of interest here?
What makes it worse is that it's now clear that we Canadians sent Mr. Peltier off to South Dakota to a travesty of a trial. The FBI agents emerge as shabby and ruthless tricksters. Vital evidence was illegally suppressed. The judge has since had a decision overturned for biased, anti-Indian remarks.
Let me conclude by reading Michele Landsberg's conclusion:
Canadian Members of Parliament of all three Parties are petitioning Justice Minister John Crosbie to intervene with Washington.
Canada, a victim of a fraud by a U.S. agency, has a right-and a duty-to ask for Mr. Peltier back. We should not, as Mr. Rosenbloom said, "sleep on our rights", but we have to do more than that if we want to shake that shadow off our national conscience. We have to look at the terms of our extradition treaties that leave us wide open to official deceit by other governments. We have to ask ourselves, is that what we mean by justice?
I hope Bill M-l 15 carries today and that we see Mr. Peltier back in Canada for a fair, open, honest and factual extradition hearing.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to my colleague from Skeena (Mr. Fulton) and I would also like to take this opportunity to thank him for presenting a motion to ask the Government of Canada to seek the annulment of the extradition of Leonard Peltier to the United States, which occurred in 1976, that is 12 years ago. Mr. Peltier was turned over to the American authorities in December 1976 after an extradition hearing was held in

September 13, 1988
Extradition
Canada. Ele was sent back to the United States where he faced charges relating to the death of two FBI officers in June 1975 and infractions he allegedly committed in other U.S. states.
This motion, Mr. Speaker, calls not only for annulment of the extradition proceedings but also for action to bring Mr. Peltier back to Canada. For that, he would have to be released, since he is now serving two life sentences for his part in murdering two FBI agents. Nowhere does it say what will happen if Mr. Peltier is allowed to return to Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the motion before you this afternoon is extremely unusual: nowhere does the law provide for annulment of extradition proceedings once a fugitive is turned over to the appropriate authorities. In fact, the motion calls upon the Government of Canada to do something that is impossible.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, it is inconceivable that the American authorities will agree to release, and thus waive their jurisdiction over, someone who was given a fair trial, found guilty and sentenced for having committed the most serious criminal offence there is.
Mr. Speaker, this particular case has, over the years, taken on near-mythical proportions. Mr. Peltier is a hero to those people in Canada, in the United Stats and in the international community who believe he was extradited on false evidence and wrongly convicted as a result of the suppression of evidence and the fabrication of testimony to convict him of crimes he did not commit. No one doubts the sincerity of the people who support Mr. Peltier's side of the case. However, the facts do not support the claims of the people who proclaim his innocence.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that we must look at the facts if we are to understand this case. In my comments on the motion I would like to examine certain important facts, and hope that many of my colleagues will do the same.
Early in 1975, Mr. Peltier went to the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota to take part in a political struggle that was taking place between the local Native government and younger members of the tribe who supported the more radical position taken by the American Indian Movement. The confrontation occurred at a time when relations between young reservation chiefs and the Indian Affairs Bureau in Washington were particularly strained. By the summer of 1975, the situation had become explosive.
On June 25, 1975, two special FBI agents, Ronald Williams and Jack Coler, came to the Pine Ridge Reservation to investigate a robbery allegedly committed by a person who was supposed to be living on the reservation.
Upon arriving in a part of the reservation called the Harry Jumping Bull Compound, the two agents were met with gun fire. The shooting came from a section of the reservation occupied by supporters of the American Indian Movement. Leonard Peltier himself did not deny his presence on the scene that day, and in January 1987, during an interview on Fifth Estate, on CBC television, he did not even challenge the
allegation that he participated in the first exchange of gun fire when the FBI agents arrived.
As soon as the first shots were fired, the two FBI agents took cover behind their vehicle. A subsequent examination of the vehicles revealed the presence of more than 125 bullet holes.
At Mr. Peltier's trial, it was proved that although the two FBI agents had been wounded during the initial exchange of gun fire, they were shot down at close range as in an execution-type shooting, with a small caliber weapon and high velocity ammunition. It was proven that Mr. Peltier was carrying a weapon of that kind that day and that he also happened to be in the area where the bodies of the FBI agents were subsequently found.
Mr. Speaker, this evidence alone is enough to justify the extradition of Mr. Peltier so that he could answer the murder charges. However, there was further evidence, a large body of evidence that implied that Mr. Peltier took an active part in the murder of the two FBI agents. It was also established that Mr. Peltier had in his possession the personal weapon of Jack Coler, one of the two FBI agents who were killed.
Although the evidence justifying the extradition of Leonard Peltier is overwhelming and conclusive, we must admit, Mr. Speaker, that we deplore the use of the two affidavits signed by Myrtle Poor Bear who claimed she saw the murder, since this flawed the proceedings. Subsequently, it was shown that Mrs. Poor Bear's testimony was entirely unreliable and that the FBI knew she had left the Pine Ridge Reservation the day before the shooting. It is unfortunate that the Canadian authorities were not informed of the problems connected with these affidavits before Judge Schultz of the British Columbia Supreme Court admitted them as evidence during the first extradition hearing early in 1976.
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today is based mainly on the fact that Mr. Peltier's extradition was obtained on the basis of the affidavits of Myrtle Poor Bear. Quite simply, this is not true. Before Mr. Peltier was handed over to the American authorities we had been advised that the testimony given by Mrs. Poor Bear was unreliable. Mr. Peltier was extradited on the basis of other admissible evidence which did warrant this course of action.
Mr. Speaker, the position of the Government of Canada is that Mr. Peltier was legitimately extradited to the United States to face charges pending against him. Moreover, no point of law would allow us to annul the extradition proceedings or seek the return of an individual serving a sentence for crimes for which he was duly found guilty.
Were such recourses possible, Mr. Speaker, nothing indicates we would be justified to act on them in this case.
September 13, 1988

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I want to start by congratulating the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) for once more introducing this important resolution. I think I should read into the record this important resolution once more. It states:
That this House deplores the extradition of Mr. Leonard Peltier to the
United States from Canada in 1976 on the basis of false information filed with
a Canadian court by American authorities, and that this House calls upon the
Government to seek the return of Mr. Peltier to Canada and the annulment of
all extradition proceedings in this regard.
Leonard Peltier is an American Indian from North Dakota. In June of 1975 he was involved in a shoot out at the Pine Ridge Reserve in the State of North Dakota. This shoot out took place as a result of two FBI agents coming to the reserve in search of a suspect, at least that is what they said. They said that they were coming to look for a suspect by the name of Jim Eagle. However, they had no warrant to go on to the reserve or to approach the ranch on the reserve where a certain number of Indians were staying. In any case, in the process of these events gun-fire broke out between the FBI agents and the Indian people. As a result of that gun-fire the two FBI agents were killed and one Indian was killed.
Following these incidents there were warrants of arrest drawn out against three of the Indians who there were there that day, a Mr. Butler, a Mr. Robideau and Leonard Peltier. Peltier escaped into Canada and was finally arrested in Hinton, Alberta in February, 1976. He was sent to Oakalla Prison in Vancouver where the extradition proceedings took place.
The proceedings started in May of 1976 and concluded in December of 1976. He was extradited to the United States where he then stood trial and was convicted of the murder of these two FBI agents.
It is interesting to note that the other two accused, Robideau and Butler, were both acquitted on the grounds of self-defence. They were all involved in this shoot out. As you know, Mr. Speaker, in a shoot out like this no one knows where the gunfire is coming from or who started it. However, at the end of it all two FBI agents were dead and one Indian was dead and warrants for arrest were issued for three people. Two of the three were acquitted, having stood trial in the United States. However Peltier was extradited from Canada to the United States, then tried and found guilty.
It was only after the extradition that it was found that one of the principal sources of evidence used against Peltier was false. That was an affidavit signed by a Myrtle Poor Bear who was allegedly the girlfriend of Leonard Peltier. In the affidavit she swore that she was at the Pine Ridge Reserve that day and that she was with Peltier and she saw Peltier fire the gun.
Later, she repudiated that affidavit and said that she was coerced. The affidavit was so discredited that it was not even
Extradition
used in the trial of Leonard Peltier when he came to trial in the United States after his extradition. The Americans themselves admitted that the affidavit was false. They accepted that. After the trial the three main witnesses against Leonard Peltier had the charges against them dropped. Two of them then stated that they were coerced to testify in the trial, and the third person died and could not comment on what took place at the trial.
Still later, through the use of the freedom of information law in the United States, it was found that the American FBI had concealed certain evidence. There was evidence that the shell casings found at the scene of the event did not come from the gun of Leonard Peltier, but from another gun. It was sworn at the trial that the shells that had shot the two FBI agents had come from Peltier's gun. First, the affidavit of Myrtle Poor Bear was shown to be a false affidavit, then the witnesses who testified against Peltier in the trial claimed that they had been coerced. Then there was the fact that certain evidence was concealed or hidden and later found to be very critical with respect to the conviction of Leonard Peltier.
On that basis there was an appeal to the American Circuit Court of Appeal to have a new trial ordered on the basis of this new evidence. It is interesting to note that the Circuit Court of the United States concluded that Peltier's defence had been hampered by the misconduct of the FBI, and by possible perjury, but it did not order a new trial. It admitted that there had been possible perjury, and it admitted that these incidents to which I referred certainly hampered Peltier's defence, but it did not order a new trial. There was a petition presented to the United States Supreme Court to order a new trial, but it turned down that request.
I am particularly incensed about this case. In 1976 when the extradition proceedings commenced, I was the Solicitor General of Canada. When the extradition proceedings were concluded, I was the Minister for Indian Affairs. During that period of time I was approached by certain Indian leaders both from Canada and the United States to intervene to have the extradition cancelled or to stop it. At the time I made inquiries with respect to this matter, but I was told that it was before the courts and justice would take its course. Something took its course, but it was not justice. It was only after the extradition and after Peltier was sent back to the United States that we found out that the affidavit was false, the evidence of the witnesses were false, and that certain evidence was concealed.
I consider this to be a travesty on the system of justice and a breach of faith between two sovereign states. Here the FBI of the United States used false evidence before a Canadian court to have an individual extradited to the United States. I consider that to be a serious breach of trust. As a Minister of the Crown at that time, I consider myself to have been misled by the authorities of the American Government.

September 13, 1988
Royal Assent
I feel that the motion put forward by my hon. colleague, the Member for Skeena, is one that must be taken seriously. I was very disappointed to hear the response of the Parliamentary Secretary speaking on behalf of the Government. He almost seemed to be building a case to justify what the Americans had done in this matter. He stated that the affidavit of Myrtle Poor Bear was not the telling evidence in this case. How are we to know? It certainly was accepted that the affidavit was false. It also came out later that other evidence was false. Surely this extradition should be annulled and be declared null and void, as the motion requests, and Peltier' should be returned to Canada for a new extradition hearing, and then there should be a new trial. Perhaps there will be enough evidence to convict him. I do not know, and I am not going to make a judgment on that. What I do know is that the extradition proceeding was false, and it should not be accepted. It is totally wrong that we here in Canada should be submitted to this type of treatment and behaviour by American authorities. I cannot understand why the Government would not take a stronger position with respect to this matter.
The type of treatment of Leonard Peltier is not an isolated case. He is only one of many Indians who have been treated unfairly by our judicial system. In a way he has become a symbol, just as Donald Marshall has become a symbol, of what is wrong with respect to our justice system in the way it relates to Indians.
It is interesting to note that, in June, 1988, the Canadian Bar Association, a rather staid and conservative organization of which I was a member at one time, put out a report entitled: "Locking up Natives in Canada: A Report of the Committee of the Canadian Bar Association on Imprisonment and Release". This report was published by Professor Michael Jackson of the University of British Columbia. In the report it states that Indians in Canada receive a raw deal before our justice system, and some radical changes should be made.
In conclusion, let me say that this case represents a serious miscarriage of justice which must be corrected. The Peltier case is an important case because of its symbolism. If we believe at all in our sovereignty as a nation, we as Canadians should make it clear to the Americans that this type of thing is not acceptable, and we should cancel that extradition.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in connection with this motion of the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). The motion states:
That this House deplores the extradition of Mr. Leonard Peltier to the United States from Canada in 1976 on the basis of false information filed with a Canadian court by American authorities, and that this House calls upon the Government to seek the return of Mr. Peltier to Canada and the annulment of all extradition proceedings in this regard.
The impact and effect of that motion is that of an application to Parliament, an application to the highest court of the land to review a proceeding that has been held and to take a fresh look at it and see if there should not be a different result. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Parliament is the highest court in the land. It means that this is the court of last resort in dealing
with problems of any nature, and problems of this type in particular.
The Hon. Member for Skeena and other Hon. Members have indicated that this particular case is one of a travesty of justice, and to quote the Hon. Member for Skeena in his quotes of others, that a fraud was committed on the judicial system. In dealing with the question of whether a fraud was perpetrated on the legal system, I suppose that we are looking at two legal systems, that of the United States and that of Canada, when we are discussing the issue. In particular, I think that Canadians generally, in viewing American courts and the American judicial system, have a tendency to feel that quite frequently American courts will go further than Canadian courts in striking down convictions of persons, whether they be native people, or otherwise, in the United States on grounds of tainted evidence.
Generally speaking, that is the impression that most Canadians have had over many years. It has only been in recent years with the Charter of Rights in this country that the Canadian courts have started to take a different attitude and a different look at the type of evidence presented and whether the evidence itself is tainted and therefore should not be allowed to be the foundation of a conviction in this country.
Having said that, as far as the Canadian courts are concerned, all Hon. Members, and particularly those who come from the legal profession, will have to agree that for a long time the American courts have been viewed much differently in this respect and have been considered as perhaps leaning a long way overboard from what Canadian courts would have done in the past with respect to dealing with evidence that was suspect in any way. That being the case, what we are being asked to do, and what apparently has been done in the United States-

That this House deplores the extradition of Mr. Leonard Peltier to the United States from Canada on the basis of false information filed with a Canadian court by American authorities, and that this House calls upon the Government to seek the return of Mr. Peltier to Canada and the annulment of all extradition proceedings in this regard.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTRADITION PROCEEDINGS REGARDING LEONARD PELTIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the break I was commenting that under our system compared with the American system, we have had a tendency over the years to feel that the American courts are much more likely to accept the fact that tainted evidence should be used to overturn a decision or strike down a trial or, in fact, not be allowed to be introduced in evidence at all so that a conviction can be founded upon it.
It appears somewhat strange to those of us who are not entirely familiar with this case and all the facts and evidence surrounding it to hear that so many people have made statements that this is a fraud committed on the judicial system in a jurisdiction like the United States where the American courts traditionally have been quite fair and much more fair, if you will, in the sense of rejecting evidence and failing to found convictions on tainted evidence or overturning a trial based on that sort of evidence.
When we are dealing with a case like this, Mr. Speaker- and we are dealing with it in the context of a court application to the highest court of the land to review it as far as we are concerned in Canada-it is only fair and reasonable that both
Extradition
sides of the argument be heard, the side of the argument which says this is a fraud committed on the judicial system and that we should, in fact, overturn it. It is also fair, I would submit, and I am sure you and all our Members would agree, Mr. Speaker, that the other side of the story should be heard in order to determine which is right and which is wrong. As well the Department of Justice has its side of the story.
As has been said, we are deciding a question here of whether Leonard Peltier was improperly convicted for the murder of Ronald Williams and Jack Coler, two special agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in the United States.
This matter has been before the courts in the United States, at trial and before U.S. appeal courts. The trial court that heard the evidence against Mr. Peltier and the various appellant courts that have examined the case in the intervening years have commented adversely upon aspects of the investigation and some of the conduct associated with the extradition and the prosecution of the case against Mr. Peltier. At the same time, notwithstanding that, the conviction has survived all of these judicial scrutinies so far in the United States.
Following Mr. Peltier's trial, and conviction in the summer of 1977, an appeal was taken to the United States Court of Appeal for the Eighth Circuit. That court upheld the conviction and subsequent appeals were similarly unsuccessful. This included a hearing before the Supreme Court of the United States.
The difficulties encountered with the affidavits of Myrtle Poor Bear continued to be an issue before the United States courts even after Mr. Peltier's conviction, although for reasons of an obvious nature, I am told, Ms. Poor Bear was not called as a witness for the prosecution at the trial. Mr. Peltier raised the affidavit issue with the Court of Appeals of the Eighth Circuit Court to underline the concerns about the way the United States investigated and prosecuted the case. It was suggested that the U.S. authorities had, in effect, presented false evidence at the extradition hearing in Canada to secure Mr. Peltier's return to the United States. The FBI was condemned by Judge Ross of the Eighth Circuit Court, who was prepared to find that the FBI had abused the investigative process by submitting the affidavits of an individual whose credibility and reliability was entirely suspect.
The judgment of Justice Ross is of interest and significance in that it demonstrates that the Court of Appeal was able to comprehend that Mr. Peltier's extradition had been justified on the basis of evidence other than the unreliable evidence contained in the affidavits sworn by Myrtle Poor Bear. It is interesting to note that when the Peltier case was before the Court of Appeals, he or his counsel did not purport to claim that he had been extradited on the basis of insufficient evidence. Mr. Justice Ross characterized the distinction in the following way:
We do not find it necessary to decide what standard should be applied to the review of claims of government misconduct in international proceedings, since, under any standard, Peltier's claim is on its face lacking in substance. Peltier does not claim that he was extradited solely on the basis of Myrtle

September 13, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Poor Bear's affidavits or that the other evidence presented to the Canadian Tribunal was insufficient to warrant extradition. It is clear from a review ... of the transcript that other substantial evidence of Peltier's involvement in the murders was presented in the extradition proceedings ...
In 1979, after exhausting the first round of conventional appeals open to him, Mr. Peltier took his case before the Eluman Rights Committee of the United Nations. By this time he was claiming that he had been unlawfully extradited from Canada on the basis of false evidence fabricated either by U.S. law enforcement officials in collaboration with Canadian authorities or by Canadian officials who acted on behalf of the Government of the United States during the extradition proceedings. He further alleged that he had been poorly treated while he was in custody in Canada and this had resulted in prejudice to his ability to prepare an adequate defence to the extradition request. Because Canada is a signatory-I notice, Mr. Speaker, that you are giving me the high sign. I will close but I would like to close by indicating that there are apparently two sides to this story. I think in fairness we should hear both sides before the highest court in the land, Parliament, makes that final decision in this particular case.
